turn_text: Well, I have been serving Alaskans now for 20 years, which is a significant period of time. And I have really had, I think, the best of all worlds coming from an extraordinary state like Alaska, a very energy rich state, but being able to focus on issues that I have long been active in whether in my previous career in Alaska, working as part of the state legislature involved with energy issues, job creation issues. But my My interest in politics really came about as one who was just always interested in my community, whether it was serving at my kids' PTA. I always say there's nothing more political than the PTA out there. but being involved in my community and then moving up to differing levels of public service. So the opportunity to serve in the Senate for a state that I love and people that I care about deeply is truly a great honor and then to lead on issues that are not only important to Alaska, but really important to the country when it comes to energy security has really been an incredible opportunity.

Great, thank you. So we've started to get to know your office a number of years back as you were working on advanced grid areas on the Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Before we get kind of into the depths of those milestones, what are some of the areas and efforts around energy that you have been and are prioritizing right now?

Well, right now, when you say prioritizing, I think it's important to recognize that when we think about energy policy and we think about how rapidly things are developing, one would think that our federal policies, our national policies also have a nimbleness to them, but far from it. When we successfully passed the Energy Act of 2020, it was the first significant energy reform bill that we had been able to advance in over a dozen years. And so when I think about priorities, It is about making sure that our energy policies are keeping up with everything that is happening around us. So I've been involved in just about every aspect of energy policy from the supply of oil and natural gas to whether or not those resources should be allowed to be exported to efficiency issues. Certainly the development of a wide range of clean energy alternatives, the infrastructure that's necessary to support it all. There's just so much out there in this energy space. And I've got kind of a, I don't know if it's a simple view of energy, but I joked about it and some, one of my former staff actually put it into a bumper sticker because I would always say energy is good. And so I keep coming back to that as kind of one of the policy guides. Energy is good, how we harness it in a way to our benefit that is consistent with environmental standards and issues, how we put it to productive use. Energy is good.

Well, Senator, it's amazing to think how much has happened in the world and in our communities since that energy act of 2020. But I did want to reflect on that a little bit. What did that achieve? Why was it so significant? How can we help continue to move it forward to advance the advanced capabilities of our electric grid?

Well, it is. Maybe I want to call it foundational or fundamental in what we were able to achieve with that Energy Act of 2020. I mentioned it was the first comprehensive update in our energy policies in about a dozen years. And so think about it just in context of of other developments. This was before the iPad even existed. That's how long a time period we're talking about since the last time we had upgraded that. And the focus was on research, R&D, development of next generation technologies to help reduce emissions, and really with a focus on what we're doing to keep energy affordable and globally competitive. We again authorized, keep in mind, because that's what the Energy Act really did, was it helped authorize these policy initiatives that really helped us work towards lowering our emissions, lowering our American energy costs, and becoming more globally competitive. And so we do this through everything from carbon sequestration, energy storage, advanced nuclear, the industrial technologies. But what we did with that was that was the authorizing, that was the foundation. But as people know, you can pass legislation authorizing something. But if you don't fund it, if you don't put the appropriations to it, you can't really breathe that life into it. And so that's where this next increment came in, which was the Infrastructure, Investment, and Jobs Act that we just passed in November that really helped to put the funding behind so much of what we had built out through that authorization in the Energy Act. of 2020.

But let's jump into the Infrastructure Act. How impactful for advancing modernization and innovation and our capabilities of our energy systems more broadly, do you feel the infrastructure packages?

Well, think about it this way. This is a generational investment in our energy and our energy innovation as well as our advanced grid capabilities. We're devoting more than $70 billion to cleaner and more resilient energy systems from renewables and micro-reactors to transmission lines. So what we've done is we have prioritized this energy infrastructure and resilience. And this is going to help communities around the country in building out cleaner and more reliable and certainly hopefully more affordable systems. And so, as we do this, you have to keep supply chain in mind and think about those initiatives that will actually work to reduce inflation as these investments are being made, because everyone's talking about inflation right now, but think about Think about what it means when you put in place these systems, whether it is your updating grid capacity, you are building out legacy investment. And that is not a contributor to inflationary spending, what we are really investing in, again, is long term and legacy. One of the points that you have mentioned about the grid, we really did prioritize the grids. I think it's really probably going to prove out to be the most consequential of measures within this bill. But we're promoting the modernization, certainly the security of our grid. It's got threats and challenges, whether from climate change or malign actors. We've got a changing energy mix. There is so much out there that is so dynamic. Some of it known, some of it really, really unknown. And so we have got to be able to be nimble. And so prioritizing this grid expansion, modernization, and security has got to be a priority for us.

turn_text: Great. Well, for our last question today, I know that you've been a champion of rolling up your sleeves and getting work done. And that often means, you know, working across the aisle. So whether it was with Senator Cantwell on the Energy Act of 2020 and others and mansion and others for the Infrastructure Act. How important do you think bipartisan work is in Congress and what hope do we have to be able to roll up our sleeves and tackle these key issues around our grid and other topics that are important to the country?

Well, I think when you're talking about initiatives where you want to put in place enduring policy, you want legacy investment. You have got to have bipartisan cooperation to help advance it. You just absolutely do. And that's not just in the energy space. It's on just about every issue out there. And I think sometimes we just don't try hard enough to try to build out the bipartisan package. It is a little bit harder, but you deliver a better product. And again, to bring it back to energy, When you think about something as fundamental to our lives, to the quality of our lives, the strength of our economy, our national security, our international competitiveness, the energy industry really occupies this space. good for anybody. It doesn't help us advance energy policy. If you've just got this pendulum that swings back and forth between elections, who's in majority, who's in control, it does nothing more than lead to a lot of lawsuits, a lot of wasted and perhaps stalled investments. But it contributes to this lack of predictability and lack of stability for the industry. So particularly in the energy space, I think bipartisan cooperation is necessary and required. And I think what we have done both in the Energy Act of 2020 as well as the bipartisan infrastructure bill. We have worked to address some longstanding challenges. We've done it in a bipartisan way. We have put in place, I think, policies that that can be counted on that can be relied on so when we talk about investments in the future from the private sector they can look at that and say okay these policies are are going to be in place here we can count on that. So, we're going to continue to do the hard stuff, which is reaching out and making sure that all the good ideas on both sides are heard. Last I checked, the Republicans don't have a monopoly on good ideas and nor do the Democrats. It's when we can come together with our ideas, recognizing that we come from different parts of the country, with different assets, different views. Let's build this together for the benefit of the country. And we've been able to demonstrate some good wins in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee. I've been proud to not only be the chairman of that committee, but the ranking member. And now I think I'm the longest serving member on that committee and not getting off at any time soon. There's too many good things happening.
